To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the expression of the mu opioid receptor (the MOR) and the analgesia and reward of morphine are altered by the persistent presence of the HIV-1 viral envelope protein (Env) in HIV-1Tg rats.
morphine use and addiction in HIV-infected individuals is associated with increased HIV-1 viral load and disease progression.

the persistent presence of the HIV-1 viral protein gp120, and to a lesser extent Tat, results in an increased expression of the MOR, and that this increase is accompanied by increased analgesic and reward responses to morphine, and increased susceptibility to the development of addiction to morphine.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the feedback interaction between the MOR and HIV-1 proteins and the mechanisms underlying the interaction.
understanding the interaction between morphine, HIV-1 viral protein expression, and HIV-1 progression to AIDS.
the feedback interaction between the expression of the morphine receptor and the function of HIV viral proteins.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there exists a feedback interaction between HIV-1 viral and MOR proteins.

morphine use and addiction in HIV-1 infected individuals is not only detrimental to the progression of HIV- 1 viral infection to the development of AIDS, but that it also has an impact on the expression of MORs and the effects of MOR ligand such as morphine.

the feedback interaction between MOR and HIV-1Tg viral proteins has not been completely characterized, however there are a number of mechanisms and processes that have been identified and that have been shown to be involved.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
morphine has a greater analgesic effect and is more reinforcing in HIV-1Tg rats than in wild-type rats.

the persistent presence of viral proteins in the brain and the peripheral nervous system, as well as the presence of viral proteins and viral proteins fragments in the bloodstream, leads to a chronic state of neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration.
HIV-1 viral protein gp120 and Tat are involved in the development of morphine dependence and the development of morphinism.
The main takeaway from our work is that

HIV-1 viral protein expression and MOR expression and signaling interact with each other and the effects of this interaction are dependent on the presence of HIV- 1 viral proteins in the brain and body.
HIV-1 viral infections and morphine use are not mutually exclusive.
there is a feedback interaction between HIV-1 viral protein expression and MOR ligand function.
